topic: Stop paying for an LLM judge
title: Stop Paying an LLM Judge: Kev-4B Local
description: Your eval suite's judge writes every verdict token by token and bills per token, so the same repeated judgments can cost thirty-four cents or twenty-eight dollars depending on who judges. This is the swap: Kev-4B, a small local decision model serving verdicts as probabilities from about nine gigabytes of GPU memory, plus the honest boundary where the big model still wins.
hook_candidates: Thirty-four cents or twenty-eight dollars, for the same 500 judgments
Kev-4B judges your agent, from 9 GB of your GPU
Stop renting a lawyer to sort your eval mail
Your eval bill is 92x too noisy, and too high
You pay per word for a verdict that is one bit
The judge does not need to write an essay
Cut your judge bill by 98.8 percent tonight
The judge flips when you swap two answers
Five hundred verdicts, thirty-four cents, local
narration_full: You score your agent's traces with a frontier API judge. Every verdict bills per token. Five hundred verdicts: thirty-four cents, or twenty-eight dollars for Claude. Look at what that bill buys. The judge, a GPT or Claude model, returns a paragraph of reasoning. Plus a JSON blob, a block of structured fields. Your software keeps a single label. The rest is generated and billed anyway. Generation brings friends. Re-score the identical trace and the verdict can drift. Swap the order of the answers and the winner can flip. That flaw is position bias. A decision model is a different shape of thing. State and typed questions go in. Probabilities come out in a single forward pass, a straight trip through the network. Calibrated means the score matches how often it is actually right. Nothing gets written. Your API judge is a courtroom lawyer, billing by the word for an opinion on every envelope. The decision model is the mail sorter, circling the routing slip at a glance. Kev four B is that sorter with open weights and an Apache license. A LoRA adapter, a small set of trainable weights on a frozen Qwen base. It serves from about nine gigabytes of GPU memory. On your own card, no API key, no meter running. Step one: clone the repository and install the server. Step two: start the judge locally with the serve command. Step three: send each trace as state plus typed questions, then read back a probability per question. Out of domain means question families it never trained on. On that locked suite, Kev four B scores zero point eight three two. Tooling is catching up, so judging every trace inside the agent loop stops being a luxury. The nightly sample retires. Here is the honest catch. You could call Kev a classifier dressed up as a judge. Date arithmetic and broad knowledge still go to the big model. It trails by a wide margin there. Date arithmetic still trips it, where its hosted sibling Jev scores higher. The sorter cannot write an opinion at all, so reasoned critique goes back to the lawyer. So tonight the same suite runs again. Every verdict comes back from Kev, on your own GPU, identical on every rerun. The judge stopped being a bill and became a download.

analogy.vehicle: hiring a courtroom lawyer to sort mail
analogy.mapping: The LLM judge bills by the word for a written opinion on every envelope; the decision model is a trained sorter that circles the routing slip at a glance.
analogy.limit: The sorter cannot write an opinion at all; anything needing reasoned critique or multi-step argument goes back to the lawyer.

notes_for_review: I anchored accuracy on Kev-4B's 0.832 instead of Kev-9B's 0.837 so the example stays on one model; confirm that reads as the intended third number phrase. The 92x-913x variance figures, the position-bias counts, and the jevals zero-dollar Kev row (an author-labeled estimate per the brief) were all dropped or rendered qualitatively to respect the three-number budget. The analogy limit is spoken verbatim in s8, and the on-screen serve commands omit the port digits for the same budget reason.
